claim: Flying across the Atlantic and back generates roughly the same carbon footprint as a typical year of commuting by car.

claim: The carbon dioxide emissions that are under the control of an individual citizen are substantially smaller than the per capita carbon footprint.
source: These carbon footprints reflect the total economic activity of a given country, so the carbon dioxide emissions that are under the control of an individual citizen are substantially smaller.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distinction between total economic activity and individual control.

claim: The per capita carbon footprint is expected to rise substantially in many countries in the developing world over the next 50 years.
source: Moreover, the per capita carbon footprint is expected to rise substantially in many countries in the developing world over the next 50 years, driven by a broad increase in the standard of living
evidence: This is a prediction based on expected economic development trends.

claim: The expected rise in per capita carbon footprint in developing countries is driven by a broad increase in the standard of living.
source: Moreover, the per capita carbon footprint is expected to rise substantially in many countries in the developing world over the next 50 years, driven by a broad increase in the standard of living
evidence: This is a causal explanation for the predicted increase in carbon footprint.

claim: Citizens in the developed world need to do all they can to start reducing carbon dioxide emissions now.
source: so citizens in the developed world need to do all they can to start reducing carbon dioxide emissions now.
evidence: This is a normative claim based on the context of rising emissions in developing countries.

claim: Most of the carbon footprint of a typical life sciences laboratory is due to refrigerators, freezers and other large items of equipment.
source: If we ignore the energy consumed in the heating and cooling of laboratory buildings – values that vary widely depending on locale – we find that most of the carbon footprint is due to refrigerators, freezers and other large items of equipment.
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of laboratory energy consumption.

claim: It takes approximately 18 kW-hours per day to operate a freezer at -80°C.
source: For example, it takes ~18 kW-hours per day to operate a freezer at -80°C
evidence: This is a specific quantitative measurement of energy consumption.

claim: Operating a freezer at -80°C translates into 4 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year.
source: it takes ~18 kW-hours per day to operate a freezer at -80°C, which translates into 4 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year (based on the US average of 1.34 pounds of carbon dioxide per kW-hour; Union of Concerned Scientists, 2012).
evidence: This is calculated from energy consumption data and a cited conversion factor.

claim: The US average is 1.34 pounds of carbon dioxide per kW-hour.
source: it takes ~18 kW-hours per day to operate a freezer at -80°C, which translates into 4 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year (based on the US average of 1.34 pounds of carbon dioxide per kW-hour; Union of Concerned Scientists, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Union of Concerned Scientists, 2012.

claim: The equipment in a typical life sciences laboratory of 7–10 people would likely generate more than 20 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year.
source: When lighting, cold rooms and smaller items of laboratory equipment (such as computers, spectrophotometers and incubators) are included, we estimate that the equipment in a typical life sciences laboratory of 7–10 people would likely generate more than 20 metric tons of carbon dioxide per year.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the authors' analysis of various laboratory equipment.

claim: It is difficult to envision how life scientists could significantly reduce the carbon footprint associated with operating their laboratories since virtually all of the energy is used to run essential equipment.
source: It is difficult to envision how life scientists could significantly reduce the carbon footprint associated with operating their laboratories since virtually all of the energy is used to run essential equipment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the essential nature of laboratory equipment.

claim: Long-distance air travel would appear to be the largest source of work-related carbon dioxide emission that the scientific community could easily reduce.
source: Thus, long-distance air travel would appear to be the largest source of work-related carbon dioxide emission that the scientific community could easily reduce.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of laboratory and travel carbon footprints and the difficulty of reducing laboratory emissions.

claim: The annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience attracts approximately 30,000 attendees to the United States from across the globe.
source: To illustrate the magnitude of the scientific community's travel-related carbon footprint, consider the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience (SFN), which attracts ~30,000 attendees to the United States from across the globe.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the size of the SFN meeting.

claim: The mean round-trip distance traveled per person at the 2014 SFN meeting in Washington, DC was approximately 7,500 kilometers.
source: By analyzing the cities of origin of attendees at the 2014 SFN meeting in Washington, DC, we estimate the mean round-trip distance traveled per person at ~7,500 kilometers
evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of attendee origin data.

claim: The 2014 SFN meeting in Washington, DC had a carbon footprint of 22,000 metric tons.
source: By analyzing the cities of origin of attendees at the 2014 SFN meeting in Washington, DC, we estimate the mean round-trip distance traveled per person at ~7,500 kilometers, which gives the meeting a carbon footprint of 22,000 metric tons
evidence: This is calculated from the number of attendees and mean travel distance.

claim: The carbon footprint of the 2014 SFN meeting is roughly equivalent to the annual carbon footprint of 1000 medium-sized laboratories.
source: which gives the meeting a carbon footprint of 22,000 metric tons, roughly equivalent to the annual carbon footprint of 1000 medium-sized laboratories.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the 22,000 metric tons from the meeting to the ~20 metric tons per laboratory estimate.

claim: All large scientific societies with an annual meeting should cut back to one large meeting every two years.
source: As a first step in reducing the carbon footprint of the scientific community we propose that all large scientific societies with an annual meeting cut back to one large meeting every two years.
evidence: This is a proposal made by the authors.

claim: A series of smaller local meetings in alternate years would bring together hundreds or thousands, rather than tens of thousands, of participants.
source: To partially compensate, we envision a series of smaller local meetings in alternate years that would bring together hundreds or thousands, rather than tens of thousands, of participants.
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposal for restructuring scientific meetings.

claim: The proposed change would roughly halve the carbon footprints associated with the largest meetings.
source: The proposed change would roughly halve the carbon footprints associated with the largest meetings.
evidence: This is an inference based on reducing meeting frequency from annual to biennial.

claim: The authors formally proposed the idea of biennial meetings to Dr. Hollis Cline, President of the Society for Neuroscience.
source: We have formally proposed this idea to Dr. Hollis Cline, President of the Society for Neuroscience, and she has agreed to put it before the Society's council.
evidence: This is a factual statement about an action taken by the authors.

claim: Dr. Hollis Cline agreed to put the proposal for biennial meetings before the Society for Neuroscience's council.
source: We have formally proposed this idea to Dr. Hollis Cline, President of the Society for Neuroscience, and she has agreed to put it before the Society's council.
evidence: This is a factual statement about Dr. Cline's response.

claim: Any proposed changes in the scheduling of large national or international meetings would likely occur on a time scale of at least 5–10 years because societies have to book convention centers many years in advance.
source: As a practical matter, any proposed changes in the scheduling of large national or international meetings would likely occur on a time scale of at least 5–10 years because societies have to book convention centers many years in advance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the practical constraints of booking convention centers.

claim: Seminars, grant review panels, interviews and other travel-intensive activities should be examined with an eye toward reducing long-distance travel.
source: We further propose that seminars, grant review panels, interviews and other travel-intensive activities be examined with an eye toward reducing long-distance travel.
evidence: This is a proposal made by the authors.

claim: For activities that do not require a face-to-face meeting, such as grant reviews, remote video-conferencing or a conference call could accomplish the same or nearly the same end.
source: For activities that do not require a face-to-face meeting, such as grant reviews, we should ask whether remote video-conferencing or a conference call could accomplish the same or nearly the same end.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the availability of remote communication technology.

claim: Scientists who do not live and work close to major scientific hubs may fear that a reduction in long-distance travel will lead to scientific isolation.
source: Scientists who do not live and work close to major scientific hubs may fear that a reduction in long-distance travel will lead to scientific isolation.
evidence: This is an inference about potential concerns of scientists in remote locations.

claim: Solutions to scientific isolation might include traveling with an itinerary that includes multiple clustered destinations and making greater use of electronic communication technology.
source: Solutions to this challenge might include traveling with an itinerary that includes multiple clustered destinations and making greater use of electronic communication technology.
evidence: This is a proposal for addressing concerns about scientific isolation.

claim: Face-to-face meetings play an important role in the life of a scientific field.
source: We appreciate that face-to-face meetings play an important role in the life of a scientific field.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment based on general knowledge of scientific practice.

claim: The cost-benefit balance of face-to-face meetings has shifted due to climate-change costs.
source: However, the cost-benefit balance has shifted: climate-change costs are long-term and they are going to be staggeringly disruptive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increasing severity of climate change impacts.

claim: Climate-change costs are long-term and they are going to be staggeringly disruptive.
source: However, the cost-benefit balance has shifted: climate-change costs are long-term and they are going to be staggeringly disruptive.
evidence: This is based on scientific consensus about climate change impacts.

claim: We are more connected now than ever before, thanks to today's technology.
source: Fortunately, we are more connected now than ever before, thanks to today's technology, so we can offset a reduction in face-to-face meetings by making greater use of electronic communication.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about modern communication technology.

claim: A reduction in face-to-face meetings can be offset by making greater use of electronic communication.
source: Fortunately, we are more connected now than ever before, thanks to today's technology, so we can offset a reduction in face-to-face meetings by making greater use of electronic communication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the availability of communication technology.

claim: With video screens simultaneously showing the speaker, the audience and the PowerPoint presentation, the remote lecture experience was remarkably similar to a live presentation.

source: Moreover, a demonstration by the scientific community that it is taking concrete action would be an important step in convincing the general public to consider similar actions.

claim: If scientists do not lead by example, then no one else will lead.
source: Conversely, if scientists – arguably the most highly educated, informed and intellectually rigorous members of society – do not lead by example, then who else will lead?
evidence: This is a rhetorical argument about the responsibility of scientists.

claim: Scientists are arguably the most highly educated, informed and intellectually rigorous members of society.
source: Conversely, if scientists – arguably the most highly educated, informed and intellectually rigorous members of society – do not lead by example, then who else will lead?
evidence: This is a characterization of scientists based on general knowledge about their training and expertise.

claim: The changes proposed are modest compared to the changes that will soon be forced upon humanity by anthropogenic climate change.
source: In summary, the changes that we propose are not small, but they are modest compared to the changes that will soon be forced upon humanity by anthropogenic climate change.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment based on predictions about climate change impacts.
